subject: Cold-start distribution mismatch propagation in continual fine-tuning without replay across domain-shifted corpora
prompt:
Topic: Cold-start distribution mismatch propagation in continual fine-tuning without replay across domain-shifted corpora

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-2497)
response:
The central question is: when you fine-tune a model sequentially on corpora from different domains — without replaying old data — how does the parameter initialization at each stage (the "cold start") interact with the distributional gap between successive domains to compound forgetting and distort the learned representations beyond what either effect would cause alone? The key concepts are catastrophic forgetting (gradient updates for new tasks overwriting weights useful for old ones), distribution shift (the statistical divergence between successive corpora in vocabulary, syntax, topic, or label schema), and cold-start mismatch specifically — the fact that the model's parameter state entering a new fine-tuning stage was shaped by a prior domain, so its loss landscape, learning rate sensitivity, and gradient directions are all miscalibrated for the incoming data before a single update is applied.

A beginner treats forgetting as a post-hoc measurement problem: you train, then you test on old tasks and observe degradation. An expert worries about the causal geometry of the weight trajectory — specifically, that a cold start in a mismatched domain drives early gradient steps in directions that are nearly orthogonal to the manifold of the new task, causing the optimizer to escape flat minima that were doing useful cross-domain work, and that this damage is done in the first few hundred steps before any learning rate schedule or early stopping could intervene. The compounding danger is that each sequential domain shift ratchets the parameter distribution further from any basin that generalizes broadly, so the effective capacity for future adaptation shrinks monotonically — a kind of representational debt that isn't visible in per-stage training loss but surfaces catastrophically when the deployment distribution differs from the final fine-tuning domain.

Freezing the bottom k layers relocates the damage more than it resolves it — the cold-start mismatch pressure doesn't disappear, it concentrates into the unfrozen upper layers, which now must absorb the entire domain adaptation signal through a fixed representational bottleneck that may itself be misaligned with the new domain. The empirical picture from adapter and partial-freeze work (Houlsby et al., 2019 on adapters; the ULMFiT gradual unfreezing results from Howard & Ruder, 2018) suggests that freezing is beneficial when the source and target domains share low-level structure — subword statistics, syntactic patterns — but becomes actively harmful when the domain shift is deep enough that the frozen layers encode assumptions the new corpus violates, because the upper layers then receive systematically distorted intermediate representations they cannot correct. Concretely, if you go from biomedical text (dense noun compounds, Latin morphology) to legal text (long-range syntactic dependencies, citation structure), the bottom layers' tokenization-level and positional statistics are mismatched enough that freezing them forces the upper layers to learn a kind of denoising task on top of adaptation, consuming capacity that should go toward task learning. The practical number that matters is the effective rank of the gradient updates in the unfrozen layers: Lee et al. (2019, "Would You Sign Up for a 5-Year Mortgage?") and later intrinsic dimensionality work (Aghajanyan et al., 2021) show that fine-tuning already operates in a surprisingly low-dimensional subspace, so concentrating updates into fewer layers further compresses that subspace, increasing the risk that sequential domain shifts drive the model out of any basin with good generalization. The subtlest harm is temporal: freezing slows the loss of old knowledge in early steps, which looks like success on short evaluation horizons, but it doesn't change the attractor structure of the optimization — the upper layers still converge to domain-specific minima, and when you unfreeze (or in the next sequential stage), the mismatch propagates downward anyway.

The asymmetry is real and general→specialized→general is the harder recovery path, for a geometric reason: general-domain pretraining produces upper layers that sit in broad, flat minima with high effective rank (they must handle diverse inputs), and specialized fine-tuning collapses that rank sharply — Aghajanyan et al. (2021) showed fine-tuning on narrow tasks reduces the intrinsic dimensionality of the weight trajectory to sometimes fewer than 200 dimensions — so when you attempt to return to general-domain fine-tuning, you're initializing from a sharp, narrow minimum that generates high-curvature loss surfaces for the broad distribution, and gradient steps are both large and poorly directed. The specialized→general→specialized path is easier because the intermediate general-domain stage, while it does overwrite task-specific upper-layer structure, tends to restore representational diversity (rank) that makes the subsequent re-specialization behave more like the original fine-tuning — essentially the general corpus acts as a soft reset toward a broader basin. Empirical support comes from Don-Yehiya et al. (2023) on continual learning with language models and from the "catastrophic forgetting is not catastrophic" experiments in Mehta et al. (2023), where models re-fine-tuned on general corpora after specialization recovered downstream task performance faster than naive sequential training predicted, suggesting the general→specialized direction destroys basin geometry more permanently than the reverse. The mechanistic reason for the asymmetry is that specialization is a contractive map on representation space — it prunes sensitivity to features irrelevant to the narrow domain — while generalization is an expansive map, and contraction followed by attempted expansion leaves you with a compressed initialization that the optimizer must first escape before it can explore, whereas expansion followed by contraction at least starts from a point with sufficient coverage. A practical signal of this asymmetry appears in learning curve shape: general→specialized→general recoveries show a characteristic long flat phase before loss drops (the optimizer escaping the sharp basin), while specialized→general→specialized curves look nearly identical to first-time specialization — the flat phase is absent or very short.

The permutation absolutely matters, and the core insight is that domain similarity is not symmetric in its effect on representational debt — fine-tuning from domain A to domain B damages the basin differently than B to A, so the optimal ordering is not simply "sort by pairwise similarity" but rather something closer to "sort by the asymmetric KL divergence of the weight trajectory distortion," which nobody has a clean closed-form for. The closest empirical work is curriculum learning research showing that ordering by increasing task difficulty reduces final loss (Bengio et al., 2009), and Shen et al. (2020) on sequential domain adaptation showed that ordering domains by decreasing overlap with the final target domain reduced catastrophic forgetting measurably — but these treat similarity as symmetric and scalar, missing the geometric asymmetry. What an expert worries about is that the optimal permutation depends on the downstream evaluation target: if you care about retaining all domains equally, you want an ordering that minimizes the maximum pairwise basin distortion (a minimax problem); if you care about the final domain only, you want the final transition to be from the most similar prior domain, and everything before that is essentially sacrificed — these are different optimization problems with different solutions. Finding the optimal permutation is in general intractable: with n domains you have n! candidates, and evaluating each requires full sequential fine-tuning runs, so even at n=8 the search space (40,320 permutations) is computationally brutal at LLM scale. The practical approximations that exist — greedy ordering by pairwise feature overlap (Nguyen et al., 2019 on transfer learning orderability), or using small proxy models to estimate transfer benefit matrices — work tolerably for n≤5 but accumulate their own approximation errors, and critically they ignore the cold-start mismatch at each stage, meaning the proxy model's estimated ordering can be wrong precisely because the proxy doesn't reproduce the basin geometry of the full model.

This is exactly what MAML (Finn et al., 2017) and its continual learning descendants are attempting, but the geometric requirement for order-invariance is more demanding than standard meta-learning delivers: the initialization needs to sit in a basin that is simultaneously flat in all directions corresponding to any domain's fine-tuning gradient, which is a much stronger condition than MAML's requirement of being close to many task-specific minima. Flatness in all domain-relevant directions means the Hessian of the loss at initialization must have small eigenvalues across the union of gradient subspaces for all domains — essentially you need a minimum whose curvature is low in a subspace whose dimension is the sum of all per-domain intrinsic dimensionalities, and if those subspaces don't overlap much (which they won't for genuinely diverse domains), you're asking for a flat region in a very high-dimensional subspace, which may simply not exist in the loss landscape of a fixed-capacity model. ANML (Beaulieu et al., 2020) and OSAKA (Caccia et al., 2021) push toward this by meta-learning not just an initialization but a modulation network that gates gradient flow per-domain, which is geometrically equivalent to carving out domain-specific low-curvature directions rather than requiring global flatness — a more tractable target. The numbers from ANML on split-miniImageNet show meaningful order-robustness, but the domains tested are far less divergent than, say, code→legal→biomedical text sequences, and there's strong reason to believe the approach breaks when domain gradient subspaces are nearly orthogonal because the meta-training objective can't simultaneously optimize for flatness in orthogonal directions without the model expanding capacity it doesn't have. Geometrically, what the ideal initialization actually needs to look like is a saddle plateau: not a minimum in the traditional sense, but a region of near-zero curvature in all task-relevant directions with controlled curvature in task-irrelevant directions, so that any domain's gradient can move the model into a good task-specific basin without first having to escape a conflicting attractor — and the closest practical approximation is sharpness-aware minimization (SAM, Foret et al., 2021) applied during meta-training, which explicitly seeks flat regions but still doesn't enforce the directionality constraint across orthogonal domain subspaces.

Yes, standard early-stopping is actively counterproductive in this setting, and the problem is more specific than "we stop too soon" — validation loss on any single held-out domain will decrease as the model finds a domain-specific sharp minimum, giving a false convergence signal precisely when the optimizer should keep moving toward the flat plateau that serves all domains. The standard early-stopping criterion (halt when validation loss stops improving) is measuring the wrong quantity: you want to track Hessian trace or the sharpness metric from SAM (the gap between perturbed and unperturbed loss, ε-sharpness), and stop when that plateaus rather than when task loss plateaus — these two events can be separated by thousands of steps, during which validation loss may actually rise slightly as the model trades sharp-minimum performance for flat-region generality. Empirical evidence for this dissociation comes from Izmailov et al. (2018) on Stochastic Weight Averaging (SWA), where averaging iterates past the early-stopping point consistently found flatter minima with better generalization, implying the standard stopping point is systematically early relative to the flat region; the performance gains from SWA were 0.5–1.5% on CIFAR and ImageNet, modest in absolute terms but mechanistically significant because they came purely from continuing past conventional convergence. The deeper problem is that flat plateaus in high-dimensional loss landscapes are not approached monotonically — the loss trajectory toward a saddle plateau often passes through regions of higher loss as the optimizer escapes sharp basins, so any patience-based early-stopping that halts on loss increase will terminate exactly at the wrong moment, interpreting the escape from a sharp minimum as divergence. What you actually need is a convergence criterion based on the stability of the gradient subspace across domains — something like measuring whether the principal components of per-domain gradients are stabilizing — but this requires simultaneous access to all domain data during meta-training, which reintroduces the replay problem that continual learning without replay was trying to avoid.

You can construct this online estimator — track the principal components of gradients from stage k using an incremental SVD (brand 2006 gives an efficient rank-1 update formula), then at stage k+1 measure the principal angle between the old subspace and the current gradient directions — but the reliability problem is fundamental: the estimate is only as good as your stage-k subspace, which was itself estimated from a single domain and therefore systematically underestimates the true multi-domain gradient subspace dimensionality, so you're measuring rotation relative to a biased reference frame that gets more biased with each sequential stage. The practical version of this idea appears in Gradient Episodic Memory (Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017) and its descendant A-GEM, which project current gradients to not conflict with stored past gradients — but these methods store gradient vectors from past data, not subspace estimates, and the distinction matters: a subspace estimated from one domain's gradients during a single training stage captures maybe 60-70% of that domain's relevant directions (based on the intrinsic dimensionality numbers from Aghajanyan et al.), meaning 30-40% of the domain's gradient structure is invisible to your rotation estimator. The stopping criterion derived from this — halt when the principal angle between consecutive-stage gradient subspaces drops below some threshold θ — would be unreliable in exactly the cases you care about most: highly divergent domains produce large principal angles throughout training (the subspaces are nearly orthogonal), so the criterion either never triggers or triggers spuriously when the current domain's gradients momentarily align with the stored subspace by coincidence rather than genuine stability. A more robust online proxy would track the variance of the principal angle across minibatches within the current stage rather than its magnitude — stable gradient subspace geometry should produce low inter-batch variance in principal angles even if the angle itself is large — but this requires storing the running subspace estimate across batches, adding O(d×r) memory overhead where r is the estimated rank, which at LLM scale (d in the millions, r potentially in the hundreds) becomes non-trivial. The honest assessment is that online subspace rotation tracking is useful as a diagnostic — it would tell you post-hoc that your stopping criterion fired at the wrong time — but as a real-time stopping signal it introduces enough noise and bias that you'd likely need to combine it with loss-based criteria and sharpness measures, at which point you have a complex multi-signal criterion that itself requires careful calibration per domain sequence.

The compression ratio — defined as the fraction of the current gradient's variance explained by projection onto the previous stage's subspace, essentially R² from regressing current gradients onto the stored principal components — is indeed a cleaner scalar than principal angle because it collapses the multi-dimensional rotation information into a single number and is more stable across minibatches, but its interpretive meaning at conventional stopping time is precisely what makes it diagnostically powerful. A high compression ratio at conventional stopping (say, >0.7, meaning 70% of current gradient variance lives in the previous subspace) means the current domain's learning signal is largely aligned with what the model already learned — geometrically, you're descending into a basin that overlaps heavily with the prior domain's attractor, which sounds safe but is actually a warning: the model may be collapsing to a shared sharp minimum rather than finding a genuinely flat region, and the conventional stopping criterion is locking in that collapse. A low compression ratio at conventional stopping (<0.3) means the current domain is pulling the model in directions almost orthogonal to prior learning — the cold-start mismatch is severe, the model is moving away from any shared basin, and stopping here leaves you in a sharp domain-specific minimum with high representational debt for future stages; this is the case where continuing training with a sharpness penalty would most help, but conventional early stopping terminates exactly here because task loss has flattened. The compression ratio's value as a stopping signal comes from tracking its trajectory rather than its instantaneous value: a ratio that starts low and rises toward 0.5-0.6 during training indicates the optimizer is finding overlap between domains that wasn't initially apparent, and stopping when this trajectory plateaus rather than when loss plateaus would better target the saddle plateau geometry. Empirical grounding for this comes obliquely from Raghu et al. (2017) on SVCCA, which showed that representational similarity between layers stabilizes at different training times than task loss, with the gap sometimes exceeding 20% of total training steps — the compression ratio is essentially a gradient-space analog of SVCCA similarity, and the same dissociation between loss convergence and geometric convergence should apply.
